[163] The Defence Pledge – for Norway's security

[164] Long-term plan for the defense sector 2025–2036 Recommendation from the Ministry of Defense on April 5, 2024, approved by the Cabinet on the same day

[165] Norway is in a serious security situation

[166] The new long-term plan for the defense sector is presented against a gloomy backdrop

[167] It is necessary to prioritize more resources for defense, security and emergency preparedness

[168] This long-term plan is a historic defense boost that strengthens our defense capabilities and allows Norway to take greater responsibility for its own security and that of its allies

[169] Norway's security policy environment has changed permanently

[170] War in Europe and the Middle East, and heightened global competition for military, political, economic and technological power characterize our country

[171] We are in a rivalry over values ​​and worldviews

[172] This new situation will be with us for a long time and has formed the basis for the choices the government has made

[173] We must expect that Norway will have to live with a more dangerous and unpredictable Russia for many years

[174] The relationship with Russia will be demanding for a long time to come, and in many ways defining for Norwegian security and defense policy

[175] The High North is Norway's most important strategic area of interest, and is becoming even more important militarily for Russia and our allies

[176] Safeguarding Norwegian interests and contributing to the greatest possible stability in our surrounding areas will require more from Norway, politically and militarily

[177] With large ocean areas, one of the longest coastlines in the world, and as a neighboring country to Russia, Norway is dependent on preserving stability and national room for action

[178] Towards Russia, our ability to combine deterrence, reassurance, predictability and long-term thinking has been important contributions to regional stability

[179] We will continue with that

[180] Climate change is contributing to increased tension and expanded areas of operation in the Arctic

[181] The economic opportunities resulting from the melting of sea ice in the Arctic are making the area interesting for an increasing number of players, and China in particular is showing increasing interest in the highlands

[182] These factors make Norway's ability to influence development in the High North even more important

[183] NATO is important to Norway

[184] The defense of Norway is based on the recognition that the security challenges exceed what Norway will be able to handle alone

[185] years in the world's strongest military and political alliance have ensured peace and been Norway's security guarantee

[186] This has given us security and greater room for manoeuvre in security policy

[187] The strengthening of the Norwegian Defence Force will support close and integrated allied cooperation and NATO as a credible and effective guarantor of Norwegian and allied security

[188] A united Nordic region in NATO is historic

[189] Finnish and Swedish NATO membership strengthens our security

[190] A new military geography is being established in our region

[191] Norway and our surrounding areas are more directly linked to the Baltic Sea region

[192] Norway's role as a recipient country of allied reinforcements is becoming more important in helping to defend NATO countries Sweden and Finland

[193] Norway is facing a more complex threat landscape than before

[194] As an open and digitalized society, Norway is vulnerable to threat actors who can threaten Norwegian interests through means that are below the threshold of military conflict

[195] The security policy situation means that the actors in total defense must be more active on a daily basis in order to jointly avert and manage threats in the transitions between peace, crisis and war

[196] The most important task of the total defense is to function in war and it must therefore train and practice in peace

[197] This also strengthens society's overall resilience and resilience to complex threats and other security-threatening activities

[198] Norway must and should take more responsibility for its own and allied security

[199] We must spend more of the community's resources on defense, security and emergency preparedness, also in the civilian sector

[200] Norway's security must be defended every day, on and outside Norwegian territory

[201] Continuous activity prevents marginalization

[202] Norwegian influence and room for action are greatest before a crisis or conflict occurs

[203] The Armed Forces shall prevent and counteract conflict in continuous and close cooperation with our allies

[204] The Government emphasizes that we should strengthen the Armed Forces in a way that gives us influence and increased national room for action to influence our surroundings

[205] This is how we ensure stability in our local areas

[206] The Armed Forces will practice and train more, with greater capacity and increased availability

[207] If conflict occurs, the Armed Forces must be able to respond in a timely manner, with relevant means of force, together with allies

[208] The Armed Forces have increased operational activity, presence in priority areas and established good situational awareness in recent years

[209] A high pace of operations over time has placed a heavy burden on the structure as a whole and, in some areas, has resulted in wear and tear on employees and a greater need for maintenance of equipment

[210] The equipment in the Armed Forces is being replaced

[211] The transition between the equipment we have and the new equipment that will be put in place sometimes challenges the Armed Forces' ability to carry out planned activities

[212] Critical deficiencies and vulnerabilities must be addressed to facilitate the initiatives proposed by the government in the defense pledge

[213] There is a gap between where we are and where current plans assumed we would be

[214] Norway has maintained a broad defense structure and invested in a modern defense

[215] Making the Armed Forces we have work is the government's first priority in this long-term plan

[216] We will acquire more ammunition, spare parts, fuel and equipment to improve preparedness and increase endurance

[217] The defense sector shall maintain and improve important infrastructure and buildings in the Armed Forces, as well as increase the capacity to receive allied forces

[218] The Armed Forces must succeed in recruiting and retaining people with the right skills

[219] The government proposes to implement a strong investment in the Armed Forces

[220] To succeed in this, several measures must be implemented simultaneously

[221] The Navy is being significantly strengthened by acquiring a minimum of five new frigates with anti-submarine helicopters

[222] A minimum of five submarines will be acquired, and a standardized vessel class in two sizes will be developed and acquired

[223] The government proposes that the Army be developed from one to three brigades and strengthened with long-range precision fire, more combat vehicles, air defense and helicopters for the land forces

[224] The special forces are being supplied with new helicopters

[225] The size of the Home Guard will increase to a total of 45,000 soldiers, and the Home Guard will be better equipped, and practice and train more

[226] Norway's protection against air threats is being significantly strengthened

[227] The radar systems are being upgraded, and more air defense batteries will help us protect more areas simultaneously

[228] This government will acquire long-range air defense for increased protection against ballistic missiles – a capacity we do not currently have in Norway

[229] To ensure that all other initiatives are effective in the Armed Forces, central joint capabilities are being strengthened within intelligence, space, digital space, and leadership, command and control

[230] The government will invest in the people in the Armed Forces through a major personnel and competence upgrade

[231] The sector will be strengthened with several thousand employees, conscripts and reservists

[232] The government will take several steps to make the personnel and competence upgrade possible

[233] More officers and commanders will be trained, efforts to retain personnel will be strengthened, more conscripts will complete their first service, and we will increase the use of reservists, who have their daily work outside the Armed Forces

[234] For the defense sector to grow, more materiel, ICT and infrastructure must be provided at the right time and in sufficient volume

[235] To achieve this, the government proposes that the possibilities for various ways to acquire new capacities be exploited, in order to get the equipment in place more quickly

[236] More procurements will be made in cooperation with allied nations, and more off-the-shelf products and similar equipment will be acquired as our allies

[237] Climate and environmental requirements must also be followed up in defense sector procurement

[238] The Armed Forces shall offer good living and working conditions to its conscripts and employees

[239] This is important for attracting and retaining people, and for accommodating employees who move or commute to perform important tasks

[240] The Government will establish sufficient housing, quarters and barracks of good quality

[241] Climate change, technological development and a more complex threat landscape are changing what is needed to defend Norway and who must cooperate to do so

[242] The Government will contribute to a more future-oriented defense sector by strengthening investment in research and development, placing greater emphasis on innovation, and strengthening work on emission reduction and climate change adaptation

[243] To finance the plan, the government is planning an escalation with a total financial scope of NOK 600 billion over a period of twelve years

[244] The escalation is achieved in particular through three significant economic boosts

[245] This is consistent with the Defense Commission's thinking

[246] Each of the three pledges is 15 billion kroner

[247] The first lift will take place as early as 2024-2025 to catch up on the backlog, make today's defense work, and increase investments

[248] The next promise will come in 2028 to facilitate the maritime initiative

[249] The last lift will take place in 2032 in order to realize the final parts of the Armed Forces' structure and a higher level of operation

[250] In addition, the plan is to escalate as evenly as possible between the three pledges, which will then amount to approximately NOK 4 billion in the years between the pledges

[251] This long-term plan is a plan for strengthening the Armed Forces that will require large resources, more employees, extensive investments and good planning

[252] The Government is therefore taking a twelve-year perspective as its basis

[253] It commits this and future governments and parliament over time, and will give the defense sector predictability to meet the significant promise

[254] The four years since the previous long-term plan was adopted show that both the security policy environment and technological conditions can change rapidly

[255] Therefore, this plan not only emphasizes predictability, but also necessary flexibility

[256] Clear choices have been made where there is the greatest certainty about the effect and where the measures will stand the test of time and in the face of change

[257] In areas with greater uncertainty, room for maneuver and the possibility of adaptation have been provided

[258] A significant use of community resources on defense requires that they be used responsibly and in line with the Storting's decisions

[259] The government is therefore making extensive changes to the management of the defense sector, and strengthening control to ensure that the escalation results in increased defense capability

[260] We are at a security policy crossroads

[261] A development that threatens our freedom of action and the international legal order requires clear political responses and priorities

[262] This long-term plan is the most important for the development of our defense capabilities in many decades

[263] The Government hereby presents the Defence Pledge – for Norway's security

[264] Part I Key developments of importance for Norwegian security and defense capabilities. Security policy developments. Our international environment is changing rapidly

[265] Our time is characterized by competition between democratic and authoritarian states

[266] China, supported by Russia, wants an alternative world order based on other values, and seeks support from countries in the global south

[267] Competition reduces opportunities for cooperation and increases the likelihood of confrontation and conflict

[268] Arms control agreements are being terminated, and a new global arms race is underway

[269] Developments are moving towards a global dichotomy with increased tension between authoritarian and democratic social models

[270] Everything indicates that the tension will last for a long time

[271] The development will challenge the institutions and cooperation mechanisms on which Norwegian security and defense are based, and Norway will be affected in an increasing number of areas

[272] In a world characterized by unpredictability and increased risk of conflict, it is important for Norway to cooperate closely with neighbors, like-minded and allied countries

[273] Norway will support an international system that continues to take into account the interests, values ​​and security of smaller states

[274] Norwegian security is greatly influenced by what happens outside the country's borders

[275] To be best prepared, we must understand the interaction between threat actors, allies, our values, and our own strengths and vulnerabilities

[276] Norway is facing a more serious threat than in many decades

[277] The danger of military conflict has increased

[278] This recognition sets the direction for national objectives, strategies, plans, capacities, structures, concepts and financial priorities in this long-term plan

[279] The greatest deterrent effect and combat power for the defense of Norway lies in allied support

[280] Norwegian authorities' cooperation with allies is crucial for the development of the unifying defense capability

[281] This is closely linked to the work to preserve the technological lead of allied countries and offset asymmetries vis-à-vis Russia and China

[282] Russia's militarization of the highlands is increasing tensions in our neighboring areas

[283] The military weakening of Russian land power as a result of the Ukraine war increases the relative importance of Russia's nuclear weapons, naval power, and air power

[284] Europe's dependence on stable energy supplies also draws military attention to the High North

[285] We must expect that Russia will meet NATO expansion with a strengthened military presence in the north and northwest, especially along the Finnish border

[286] Climate change also affects the security situation in the High North

[287] With rising temperatures and reduced sea ice, the region is becoming available for civilian and military activity for longer periods of the year and for more actors

[288] Climate change will open up larger areas of operation in the High North and create new challenges and opportunities for Norway, our allies and Russia

[289] The understanding of the concept of security has been expanded

[290] Security threats and challenges are not only military, but increasingly also linked to the use of complex instruments and complex threats

[291] An increasing number of states and actors are acquiring the capacity to carry out disruptive and destructive cyber operations targeting critical infrastructure and national government functions

[292] We must be prepared that Norway may be affected to a greater extent, and with greater consequences, than we have seen so far

[293] Other states use several instruments to influence Norwegian and allied policies and freedom of action

[294] This means that Norwegian authorities must implement countermeasures within a broader, and often allied, framework

[295] NATO's strategic concept reflects this development, and is the starting point for jointly meeting challenges to allied security

[296] Through its attack on Ukraine, Russia has violated international law and demonstrated a willingness to use extensive and ruthless military force to achieve its goals

[297] Russian military power remains the defining challenge to Norwegian and allied security in Europe

[298] This means that Norway must be better prepared for a more dangerous and unpredictable Russia

[299] In the short term, the war has weakened Russia militarily, but the country's ability to transition to a war economy makes it dangerous to underestimate Russian combat power, even in the near future

[300] This is reinforced by China's willingness to compensate for the collapse of Russia's trade with Europe, and China's direct and indirect support for the reconstruction of the Russian defense industry

[301] China seeks to control strategic infrastructure, resources and value chains, and increasingly poses a systemic security challenge for Norway and Europe

[302] China is working purposefully to weaken the United States and the West's freedom of action in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific region

[303] The potential for conflict related to Taiwan, the South China Sea and the Korean Peninsula is increasing

[304] China's military buildup and assertive behavior, along with North Korea's development of longer-range nuclear weapons, are pressuring other Asian countries to build a credible deterrent

[305] Climate change, population growth, war and resource scarcity mean that we must be prepared for unrest and larger refugee flows

[306] The UN, NATO and the EU must take into account pressure on Europe's external borders and the possibility of military action along Europe's borders

[307] Migration can affect political and social stability in Europe

[308] Increased instability could also contribute to further military buildup

[309] States or other actors who wish to challenge state and societal security can use a number of tools that fall below the threshold of armed conflict

[310] Overt and covert diplomatic, informational, military, criminal, economic, financial, intelligence and legal means are increasingly being used to achieve strategic objectives

[311] The likelihood of terrorist attacks by individuals or centrally controlled networks is changing rapidly

[312] Simple attacks carried out by individuals still pose the greatest terrorist threat in Europe and Norway

[313] An increasing number of armed conflicts serve as potential combat training arenas

[314] More armed conflicts can also lead to more state-sponsored terrorism

[315] This can, for example, come in the form of state-sponsored cyberattacks, assassinations and other forms of terrorist attacks

[316] The war between Israel and Hamas in the Middle East and Iran's central role have increased the likelihood of terrorism affecting Norwegian and allied interests

[317] Security policy challenges

[318] The rivalry between the great powers is increasing and will likely persist

[319] Instability, the risk of unwanted escalation and states' use of force to impose their will on others are once again relevant in our part of the world

[320] Compounding threats and technological developments are compounding the challenge

[321] These developments make it more demanding, but at the same time more important, to actively safeguard Norwegian security, our security policy space and our security interests

[322] The strategic importance of the High North

[323] The High North is Norway's most important strategic area of ​​interest

[324] The government's goal is to contribute to predictability and stability in the High North

[325] In a turbulent time with increased interest in the High North from an increasing number of states, Norway must have the ability to understand, influence and shape developments in the region

[326] This requires that we have a continuous presence in the High North with relevant capacities

[327] We must be clear about what our interests in the Arctic are, and the importance of Arctic and non-Arctic states supporting international law

[328] The High North has long been a peaceful and stable region, characterized by cooperation, mutual trust and compliance with international laws and regulations

[329] This is still Norway's long-term goal

[330] At the same time, we must acknowledge that the High North is increasingly affected by geopolitical tensions

[331] The Arctic could become an arena for competition between the great powers, where the increasing cooperation between Russia and China in particular could have a major impact on the region's further development

[332] The High North has gained increased strategic importance, both as a result of the serious security situation and because the sea ice in the Arctic is melting

[333] Norway is a maritime frontline state in NATO

[334] For Russia, the region has great value because the country has stationed significant parts of its nuclear retaliation capacity on the Kola Peninsula

[335] It is very important for Russia to protect this capacity and the area of operation for Russia's strategic submarines, such as the ice-free shipping route into the Norwegian Sea and the North Atlantic

[336] Russia's access to the open seas in the north indicates that the military-strategic importance of these sea areas will increase further

[337] Especially because the Baltic Sea is now dominated by NATO countries

[338] We must therefore expect that Russian military activity in the High North will continue

[339] Access to the Atlantic Ocean and defense of the northern bastion are crucial in Russian security thinking

[340] Russia continues to test and develop advanced weapons systems in the High North, and military exercise activity in the region has been high for several years

[341] In connection with Russian exercises on the Kola Peninsula, there have also been disruptions to GPS signals that have affected Norwegian civil aviation and emergency preparedness

[342] Russia is also using military capabilities deployed in the north, such as strategic bombers, in the warfare against Ukraine

[343] doctrine defines the Arctic as a vital area, and Russia has passed a law on control of foreign state vessels in the Northeast Passage

[344] A possible development of the Northeast Passage for commercial traffic could in the future shorten sailing times to European markets, reduce dependence on other shipping routes and facilitate the extraction and transport of natural resources

[345] Overall, this indicates that the Northern Fleet and the highlands will continue to have crucial strategic importance for Russia

[346] Russia's defense plans will likely be adjusted as a result of Sweden's and Finland's NATO membership

[347] NATO's border with Russia is becoming longer, and the Arctic is being linked more closely to the Baltic Sea area

[348] Russia has already expressed ambitions to establish several new military units along the new NATO border, as well as to reorganize the military districts in the north and west

[349] Norway's coastline stretches along large Arctic sea areas, with easy access to the Barents Sea and the North Atlantic

[350] Our allies are increasingly linking their own security to developments in the High North

[351] Therefore, they are also showing greater interest in developments in the Arctic

[352] They are increasingly present in the region to gain better situational awareness and to send strategic signals to Russia

[353] Allies are particularly interested in developments that could challenge Norwegian and allied security

[354] This applies in particular to Russian developments in the underwater domain; the Barents Sea as a test area for new Russian weapons systems; the modernization of nuclear weapons and long-range precision weapons

[355] Through exercises, Russia has clearly demonstrated its ability to disrupt allied supplies across the Atlantic

[356] This poses an ongoing strategic challenge for both Norway and our allies

[357] Threats and challenges to undersea installations and cables on which modern society depends have also received increased attention

[358] Increased allied cooperation and presence in the form of training and exercises in the High North is positive for Norwegian security

[359] At the same time, total military activity should be at a level that facilitates the government's goal of predictability and stability in the High North

[360] The government wants to increase Norwegian influence and influence on allied activity in our immediate areas, and increase understanding of Norwegian security policy priorities among our allies

[361] The challenges are exacerbated by the fact that climate change is occurring particularly rapidly in the highlands

[362] The temperature in the Arctic is increasing four times faster than the global average

[363] The warming of the Arctic and rapidly melting sea ice have led to an increase in civilian shipping traffic in the sea areas around Svalbard

[364] Rising ocean temperatures in the Arctic have the potential to change ecosystems from which Arctic states benefit economically

[365] For example, radical changes in the climate in Svalbard are expected towards the end of this century

[366] The melting of the ice could contribute to increased commercial and military activity in the form of greater interest in natural resources, new sailing patterns and changes in the military presence in the region

[367] Climate change has long been considered a threat multiplier

[368] This implies that climate change affects conditions that can help expand or complicate existing threats

[369] Climate change could affect military installations, capacities and operations, and create challenges that could contribute to war and conflict

[370] Thus, climate change is increasingly also an independent security challenge and a threat to national, regional and global stability

[371] Any increase in civilian and military activity in the High North increases the risk of accidents and emissions

[372] Norway and other Arctic coastal states must therefore be prepared for the consequences of increased activity

[373] For example, it will require capacity for incident management within search and rescue, fisheries management and environmental pollution

[374] The melting ice is helping to expand the operational area of the Armed Forces and especially the Coast Guard

[375] Greater activity from Russia, China and allies also increases the need for Norwegian presence and influence in our surrounding areas

[376] Reduced or absent sea ice can change military action patterns and presence in the region, and can also affect the sailing patterns of strategic submarines

[377] Climate change places increased demands on Norwegian preparedness, response capacity and presence

[378] The armed forces' infrastructure, materiel and logistics must be adapted

[379] Norwegian military planning must take more account of more frequent extreme weather, higher sea levels and reduced sea ice extent

[380] This may also affect the availability of training areas for national and allied forces

[381] International rivalry is simultaneously increasing the strategic importance of outer space

[382] Space technology can be utilized for surveillance, intelligence, and target selection, among other things, and will be crucial for conducting effective military operations

[383] Space-based capabilities are becoming increasingly important for maintaining NATO's freedom of action in the High North

[384] Satellite systems have increased in importance for Norway's and NATO's security

[385] Thus, redundancy and backup solutions for space-based technology are becoming increasingly important

[386] Norway's unique geographical location, our expertise and capacity in the development and launch of satellites, as well as downloading satellite data, give Norway comparative advantages in cooperation with the US, the EU and other allies

[387] The government expects that Norway will have a more central role in the exploitation of space in the future

[388] This is explained in more detail in Chapter

[389] China is also showing increased interest in the Arctic

[390] China considers itself a "near-Arctic state", seeks influence through investments and will likely position itself for future opportunities

[391] China is particularly interested in shipping routes, extraction of natural resources, space-based capabilities and research

[392] It is to be expected that China will become an increasingly important partner for Russia in the Arctic, as Russia is increasingly dependent on China to achieve its ambitions in the region

[393] China has a great interest in multi-purpose technology, and systematically exploits access to civilian technology for military purposes

[394] China's activity in the High North is still limited, but the last decade's voyages with state-owned icebreakers in the Arctic enable the country to operate more independently in the region

[395] China has so far not challenged the provisions of the law of the sea in the Arctic

[396] However, it cannot be ruled out that China's increasing global power positioning could in the long term lead to a Chinese military presence in the Arctic

[397] An agreement was recently signed between the Chinese and Russian coast guards

[398] This is an example of concrete Sino-Russian cooperation that could have consequences in the Arctic

[399] An increasing number of non-Arctic states are showing increased interest in the High North

[400] This is particularly about making trade routes and natural resources accessible

[401] There is increased interest in climate research, and an increasing number of Arctic and non-Arctic states have prepared Arctic strategies or similar documents

[402] This includes close allies such as the United States and the United Kingdom, but also Russia and China

[403] Russia's development Russia today poses the foremost threat to Europe, Norway and Norwegian interests, and remains the defining factor in shaping Norwegian security and defense policy

[404] It must be assumed that this will persist

[405] The relationship between NATO and Russia is characterized by confrontation, and intervenes in all domains and geographical areas where Russian and allied interests meet

[406] Russia is now strengthening its cooperation with non-Western countries to challenge what Russia refers to as Western hegemony, and seeks to build an international order that better safeguards Russian interests

[407] China will become increasingly important to the threat Russia poses to NATO and allied countries

[408] The Russian regime has shown a willingness to use extensive and ruthless military force to achieve its political goals

[409] Russia has clear totalitarian traits, wants to revise the current distribution of power and security architecture, regularly violates its international obligations, acts in violation of basic human rights, and does not recognize the right of sovereign states to self-determination

[410] Russian society is becoming increasingly militarized, brutalized, and permeated by the Putin regime's propaganda against regime critics and "hostile" states

[411] The Putin regime seems to aim to restore the Soviet Union's great power status

[412] Despite some uncertainty about the regime's stability, there is little indication of an imminent change in political course in Russia

[413] Regardless of how the war in Ukraine ends, Norway and the West must be prepared for a more dangerous and unpredictable Russia

[414] This will influence political choices for a long time to come

[415] The war in Ukraine has reinforced Russia's need for strategic dominance in the Arctic and its ability for global and regional power projection

[416] The Russian defense concept implies that Norway and nearby Norwegian areas may be located completely or partially behind Russian defense lines

[417] The strategic importance of the Arctic Circle increases as a result of Finnish and Swedish NATO membership, not least because Norway becomes an important gateway for Allied reinforcements and supplies to Finland and Sweden

[418] While Russia increasingly appears as a threat, the war in Ukraine entails major political, economic and military costs

[419] The invasion of Ukraine revealed unexpected weaknesses in Russian military power, including in terms of materiel, joint operational capability, command and control, and logistical support

[420] Russian military capabilities in our immediate vicinity are currently significantly reduced, particularly within conventional land forces and air defense

[421] It will take time and resources to rebuild this

[422] A weakened Russia is not necessarily a less dangerous Russia

[423] Although Russia is weakened in some areas, this is most likely a temporary situation

[424] Since the invasion began, Russia has shown increasing ability to develop military capabilities faster than expected

[425] The country has converted to a war economy and significantly increased the production of military equipment and ammunition

[426] In 2024, Russia will spend about a third of its state budget on defense and security, which amounts to about six percent of the country's GDP

[427] How quickly Russia rebuilds its military capability will be determined by developments in the Russian economy and the effect of international sanctions

[428] Russian GDP has remained relatively stable, although the prospects for continued economic growth are uncertain

[429] The further development of the defense force also depends on how much, and what kind, support Russia receives, primarily from China, but also from Iran and North Korea

[430] Chinese deliveries of military equipment and components are crucial to Russia's warfare in Ukraine

[431] China supports the arms industry with machinery, electronics and parts

[432] Russia gains significant combat experience in Ukraine and can test out concepts, capabilities, and technology

[433] The temporary weakening of Russian conventional capabilities simultaneously increases Russia's emphasis on nuclear weapons and the use of composite instruments

[434] Russia will continue to prioritize strategic deterrence forces, especially strategic and multi-role submarines and advanced long-range precision weapons

[435] Russia's threats to use nuclear weapons may help lower the threshold for nuclear escalation

[436] This also applies to our surrounding areas

[437] Any conflict between Russia and NATO will have a nuclear dimension

[438] In the coming years, we must also expect testing and development of high-priority weapons systems such as new long-range precision weapons, ballistic and hypersonic missiles, and anti-satellite weapons

[439] Russian naval and air power in the north is still intact, and it must be taken into account that a politically and economically weakened Russia will become more unpredictable and risk-averse

[440] Both before, during and outside of armed conflict, Russian use of covert means will be likely

[441] The prime example of this is the use of energy as a means of pressure, but the threat to critical infrastructure has also increased

[442] It is important for Russia to deter allied countries from providing further support to Ukraine

[443] Russia's complex use of instruments against Western values, critical infrastructure and socially critical resources aims to spread unrest and fear among the population of Europe and create division within, and between, Western countries

[444] Russia has shown great willingness and ability to use instruments below the threshold of armed conflict

[445] This applies in particular to activities related to influence and information operations, sabotage and intelligence in and outside the digital space, and in the form of, for example, electronic warfare

[446] The consequences of the Ukraine war and the deep ideological contradiction between the Putin regime and the West may increase the scope and frequency of this form of use of force even after the war is over

[447] In the long term, we must also take into account that Russia will further develop its military technological expertise, and increasingly use AI technology, hypersonic missiles, autonomous systems and drone technology

[448] Russia is already investing in capabilities in outer space, and the development of anti-satellite weapons has been a priority

[449] In important areas, Russia will likely seek to compensate for brain drain and deficiencies in its own defense industry by increasing cooperation with countries such as China, Iran, and North Korea

[450] Norwegian authorities have very limited bilateral contact with Russia

[451] In the area of ​​security and defense policy, certain points of contact have been maintained to ensure a necessary minimum of risk reduction

[452] Along with openness about one's own military activity and political intentions, such contact surfaces are particularly important in periods of high tension, but also to support the long-term goal of stability and predictability in our immediate areas

[453] Ukraine's defensive struggle

[454] The outcome of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has direct and decisive significance for Norwegian and allied security

[455] If Russia learns that military force is an effective political tool, this will threaten the norm of non-aggression and peaceful conflict resolution that has prevailed in Europe

[456] This norm is particularly important for Norway

[457] Ukraine is defending not only its own country, but also international law and Western democratic values

[458] It is crucial that Russia's aggression does not prevail

[459] Norwegian security interests are therefore best served by providing effective military support to Ukraine

[460] Russian threats of escalation do not change this

[461] The war in Ukraine has become a war of attrition with high intensity and heavy losses on both sides

[462] The armed conflict began as early as 2014, but was greatly expanded when Russia launched a full-scale invasion on February

[463] The war seems to be a long one

[464] Until the spring of 2024, neither country had sufficient strength to achieve a decisive breakthrough

[465] A negotiated end to the war on terms acceptable to Ukraine will only be possible if Russia perceives Ukraine's defense capabilities as so strong that Russian objectives cannot be achieved through further warfare

[466] Ukraine will need military support for a long time to facilitate this

[467] Long-term, comprehensive and coordinated support will be required in the form of military equipment, training, supplies and repairs

[468] The reconstruction of Ukrainian society will require enormous resources

[469] Deterrence and appeasement During the Cold War, Norway developed a security strategy that aimed to combine deterrence and appeasement towards the Soviet Union with a policy of integration and containment towards the USA and NATO

[470] Both deterrence and reassurance are strategies intended to avoid an attack or a serious pressure situation

[471] Through NATO, bilateralization could be avoided by the United States stepping in on the Norwegian side if war broke out between Norway and the Soviet Union

[472] At the same time, Norway demonstrated, through words and actions, a clear desire to maintain a low level of tension in the North

[473] The main elements of this policy were

[474] the base policy; the nuclear and port policy; and restrictions on allied military activity, especially in Finnmark

[475] These were mainly continued towards Russia after the end of the Cold War

[476] The base policy was a unilateral Norwegian declaration that came in connection with Norway's entry into NATO

[477] In an exchange of notes with the Soviet Union, the then Norwegian government stated that Norway would not "enter into any agreement with other states that entails obligations for Norway to open bases for the combat forces of foreign powers on Norwegian territory as long as Norway is not attacked or exposed to threats of attack

[478] The Norwegian government decided unilaterally in 1957 that nuclear weapons would not be deployed on Norwegian soil in peacetime

[479] A further clarification of nuclear weapons policy came with the Bratteli Doctrine in 1975, which states that Norwegian authorities assume that nuclear weapons are not carried on board when foreign warships call at Norwegian ports

[480] Successive Norwegian governments have combined deterrence measures with measures intended to appease the Soviet Union and Russia, so that the sum of Norwegian policies has the greatest possible risk-reducing and stabilizing effect in our immediate areas

[481] The practical policy formulation has emphasized a flexible approach

[482] Reference is often made to a "balance" between deterrence - showing the other party that there will be consequences for attacking Norway, and reassurance - showing the other party that neither Norway nor NATO has aggressive intentions

[483] Deterrence and reassurance should not be perceived as mutually exclusive quantities or a pair of concepts that presuppose a “balance”, in the sense that more deterrence would presuppose a corresponding reduction in “reassurance”, or vice versa

[484] These are rather scalable quantities, where the effect of political instruments can be adapted to needs and situations with the aim of achieving the desired effect

[485] The base policy, the port call and nuclear weapons policy, and the approach to foreign military presence and activity in the border areas with Russia are concrete expressions of Norwegian application policy

[486] This government believes that the long lines of Norwegian security policy create predictability and increase our ability to influence our local areas

[487] In the face of a more unstable and unpredictable security policy situation, allied unity and stability in the High North are increasingly important

[488] At the same time, facilitating increased allied military activity in the North has long been a central part of Norwegian security and defense policy

[489] Reinforcement in crisis and conflict must be practiced and prepared in peace to be effective in crisis and war

[490] This increases the need for allied activity in Norway and nearby Norwegian areas

[491] The government wants to increase the Armed Forces' ability to operate together with allied forces in Norway and nearby Norwegian areas

[492] As the potential for conflict in our areas has increased, our ability to understand, shape, coordinate, and participate in activities in our areas becomes more important to prevent escalation

[493] Finnish and Swedish NATO membership and closer Nordic cooperation will affect security and stability in our region and the threat perception on the Russian side

[494] Norway must take into account the need to underpin Western unity and promote joint deterrence of Russia in the North and in the Baltic Sea region

[495] The government's goal of not acting unnecessarily provocatively in the north remains

[496] Norwegian policy should continue to aim to reduce the risk of unnecessary escalation and contribute to predictability and stability in relations with Russia, without this being at the expense of Norwegian security interests

[497] Allies and Western partner countries must plan and size their own capacities for continued support of Ukraine

[498] At the same time, Russia's behavior towards its neighbors has created a great need to modernize and equip European defenses

[499] The war in Ukraine is therefore a very important factor for developments in NATO and for the defense plans of allies and partner countries

[500] Ukraine's defensive struggle has demonstrated the importance of the resilience of the population, the fighting spirit of the soldiers, and good leadership

[501] Civilian support for military efforts and resilience in civilian sectors has been important

[502] The war has also shown that long-range precision weapons and good air defense cover play a crucial role

[503] To resist a conventional attack, high-tech weapons and good communications infrastructure are needed

[504] It is also crucial to have access to artillery, effective air defense, drone capacity, sufficient ammunition, robust logistics systems, as well as the ability to quickly mobilize, reinforce, replace and regenerate one's own forces

[505] The war has also demonstrated the importance of a robust defense industry with the ability to rapidly increase production, capable of supplying the Norwegian and allied defense sectors

[506] This requires close cooperation between authorities and the private sector

[507] Supply chains are often multinational

[508] Therefore, close coordination between allies and like-minded countries is absolutely necessary

[509] Military support for Ukraine is channeled through the defense budget, with funding through various multinational mechanisms

[510] The expenses are high

[511] Therefore, it is important to have separate funding so that the support does not come at the expense of the defense of Norway

[512] Box 1.2 The Nansen Programme and Norwegian support to Ukraine

[513] The defense sector has contributed significant donations of materiel to Ukraine's defense struggle after the Russian attack

[514] Norway's multi-year support program for Ukraine: – NOK 75 billion in the period 2023–2027, plus NOK 5 billion to the global south in 2023. – NOK 10 billion for military support in 2023, including the value of defense equipment to be reacquired. – NOK 7.5 billion for civilian support

[515] – Future priorities, including how the distribution between civilian and military support will be distributed from 2024 onwards, will be promoted in the annual budget processes

[516] Objectives of the Norwegian support

[517] – Ukraine should be able to decide its own future

[518] – Ukraine's needs should form the basis for Norwegian support

[519] – The support will be coordinated with Ukrainian authorities and international partners

[520] – The Nansen program must ensure a clear distinction between military and civilian support

[521] – The Nansen program will emphasize documented delivery capabilities and good control systems

[522] In the case of donations of equipment that the Armed Forces still use, thorough assessments have been made of the consequences for national preparedness

[523] Until now, the temporary reductions in the Armed Forces' readiness have been considered acceptable in light of Ukraine's acute need for such equipment

[524] As a general rule, donated equipment is re-acquired as quickly as possible, and ongoing assessments are made regarding mitigating measures to maintain national preparedness

[525] The rise of China

[526] China is the world's second largest economy and Europe's largest trading partner

[527] China has significantly strengthened its military capacity and ability to exercise global power in recent years

[528] Norwegian and allied security is increasingly affected by China's rapid rise and increasingly assertive behavior

[529] China's growing power, broad set of instruments, and willingness to use them

[530] has consequences regionally, globally and for national security

[531] China and Russia do not always have coincident interests or goals

[532] However, they are united by a common desire to establish an alternative international order, weaken America's international leadership, divide Western countries, and create realities and rules of engagement that are aligned with Chinese and Russian interests and governance

[533] At the same time, it is a core Norwegian interest to counteract attempts to challenge and undermine international law, universal human rights and the multilateral system

[534] As a consequence of this, and in light of growing allied concern, China has also been elevated to the NATO agenda

[535] Since 2019, NATO has increased its focus on complex threats from China, and how the country's growing conventional and nuclear capabilities could challenge the alliance

[536] The interaction between China and Russia is of increasing importance for the threats Norway and NATO face, but also for how the allies choose to meet and handle such challenges

[537] China's extensive support for Russia's warfare in Ukraine is a subject of growing concern in Norway and NATO

[538] China also affects Norwegian security by drawing American resources and attention away from Europe

[539] Norway and our European allies have an independent interest in stability in the Indo-Pacific region

[540] Both to maintain trade and supply lines, and to counteract and avoid conflicts that could lead to the risk of spread

[541] For the United States, China is the decisive and defining security challenge

[542] Developments in the Indo-Pacific region are of central importance in the international context, and are increasingly affecting the security situation in the Euro-Atlantic area

[543] This is primarily because US policies and behavior in Europe and other regions reflect US goals and interests towards China

[544] The Norwegian and European authorities' policy towards China is therefore increasingly important for how the United States views NATO and the costs of supporting European security

[545] It will be important that European countries contribute to NATO remaining relevant in the face of a world increasingly dominated by the rivalry between the United States and China

[546] China's more forward-looking and confident behavior in Asia is also becoming increasingly important for Norway

[547] The United States' leading international position is based on the country's role as both an Atlantic and Pacific power

[548] China's growing power therefore makes the United States more dependent on interaction with allies and partner countries

[549] It also leads to the risk that the Indo-Pacific region will become a China-centric region, where other countries will have to take Chinese goals and interests into account, whether they want to or not

[550] America's allies and partners in the region want to counteract such an outcome, and are engaging in various ways in the establishment of a regional security architecture, which will help ensure that the United States remains a central power in the region

[551] Japan, Australia and South Korea in particular are contributing to this, and are helping to draw Western-oriented countries in the region closer to NATO, Europe and Norway

[552] The rivalry between the United States and China has an inherent potential for conflict

[553] The security dynamics around Taiwan, in the South China Sea, and on the Korean Peninsula are increasingly worrying

[554] The risk of misunderstandings and unintentional escalation increases

[555] China is also seeking increased control over the South China Sea, while the United States and its allies emphasize the principle of freedom of navigation at sea

[556] China is also challenging Japan in the East China Sea

[557] North Korea's steps towards establishing itself as a full-fledged nuclear weapons power are contributing to the riskier developments on the Korean Peninsula

[558] Should military conflict arise, this would have major geopolitical, security policy and economic repercussions

[559] Norway's intelligence and security services emphasize how China, together with Russia, challenges other nations' security interests across areas of society

[560] China's primary instruments of influence in Europe are economic, and there are several examples of China exploiting Western dependence on Chinese markets, supply chains, transportation and logistics networks to challenge Western interests and room for maneuver

[561] In addition, China systematically uses research and development cooperation as a means of building its own military capacity

[562] Chinese means also include the use of cyber actors

[563] China operates long-term and uses a wide range of actors and instruments to achieve its political goals

[564] According to the Chinese Intelligence Law of 2017, Chinese authorities can order Chinese businesses, research groups, media and individuals to cooperate with and hand over information to Chinese intelligence

[565] In addition, Chinese businesses are linked to the authorities through party committees, financing, part-ownership, board representation, joint ventures, or collaborative agreements on research and innovation

[566] China's absent dividing lines between politics and economics, public and private sectors, and between civilian and military spheres provide unique opportunities for comprehensive and coordinated use of instruments

[567] China is Norway's most important trading partner in Asia, central to global value chains and important for achieving climate and sustainability goals

[568] The Government will therefore cooperate with China where it is in our interest, while at the same time exercising increased caution in cooperation with China and Chinese actors if it affects matters related to national security

[569] National security interests and alliance commitments should be the basis, while we work for long-term economic interests, support for a world based on international law, and global climate and sustainability goals

[570] The government wants to follow a Nordic and European line

[571] This way, we will also be less exposed to pressure while standing up for Norwegian social values and international human rights

[572] The government will have a calibrated approach to China, based on risk reduction and identification of areas where cooperation poses unacceptable risks to Norwegian or allied security

[573] The Global South

[574] The government sees the contours of a more bloc-divided world in which the global south is making its presence felt

[575] The term "global south" is used to refer to a very complex and diverse group of states in several continents, with many different interests and perspectives

[576] New collaborations are constantly developing between rapidly growing economies in the global south

[577] Several of these support China's alternative international order

[578] China's market position in the south is strengthened by Chinese businesses using and promoting Chinese technical standards

[579] China's loans and investments in the global south are significant

[580] Access to critical minerals and metals is key, and Chinese investments in infrastructure, factories and mining will remain important for building economic and political alliances

[581] The BRICS cooperation forum was established in 2009 and expanded in

[582] Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa have now been joined by Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates

[583] This is a very complex group of countries, where there are also strong conflicts of interest and values ​​between several of the member countries

[584] The forum aims to strengthen the conditions for developing countries in international politics and economics

[585] The BRICS countries now represent 45 percent of the world's population and some of the world's most important oil exporters

[586] Several of the member countries see the forum both as a means of strengthening their own influence internationally, and as an alternative to the G7 and other international institutions and cooperation based on democratic values

[587] This development could contribute to increasing international tension

[588] Terrorism remains a challenge in parts of the global south

[589] Both ISIL and al-Qaeda prioritize areas with conflict and weak government control

[590] Organizations use their global networks to transfer capacity between different areas

[591] In sub-Saharan Africa, both ISIL and al-Qaeda are expected to strengthen

[592] They ally with local groups to gain ground and to appear as ideological focal points that offer security, services, and a competing vision

[593] A common denominator for the challenges in the Middle East is Iran's central role

[594] Iran is attempting to increase its own influence in the region by playing on various militia groups, states and actors

[595] An escalation of the conflict in Yemen, where Iran and the Gulf states are on opposite sides, could have serious regional consequences

[596] Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza has consequences for the region, for Western support for Ukraine, and for Western countries' ability to win support among countries in the global south

[597] The dispute between Iran and the United States is being fought through proxies, as Iran seems to want to avoid direct conflict with the United States

[598] The relationship between Russia, Turkey, Iran and the United States is crucial for developments in Syria

[599] A Russian escalation in Syria will make the Assad regime more dependent on Iran

[600] Iraq is economically and security-wise dependent on both the United States and Iran, and the security situation in Iraq is directly affected by the relationship between the two countries

[601] The areas south of Europe are among those that will feel the consequences of climate change first, and are the least equipped to meet them

[602] If vulnerable countries experience major negative consequences from climate change, the risk of political instability, humanitarian disasters and violent conflict increases

[603] Population growth, famine, extreme weather and water shortages can lead to refugee flows, but also terrorism and war

[604] This could also create cooperation challenges and have a destabilizing effect on Europe

[605] Climate change and more climate-related disasters are expected to lead to more involuntary migration and forced displacement

[606] The strong population growth in parts of Asia, Africa and Latin America will exacerbate climate-related challenges

[607] Climate change could affect weather systems, sea levels, biodiversity and global temperatures, but also food security and global health

[608] The result could be refugee flows that challenge social and political stability

[609] Wars and conflicts caused by climate change may create a need for more assistance for civilian and military crisis management

[610] Composite threats

[611] Traditionally, peace, crisis, and war have been considered as steps along a scale of severity

[612] Such steps are easy to understand, but may provide an inaccurate representation of the new security situation

[613] Norwegian security is continuously challenged, both directly and indirectly, by multiple actors, in multiple arenas, and with a variety of instruments

[614] Although there is a distinction between peace, crisis and war, the transitions between them have become less clear and more dynamic

[615] Today's security situation is characterized by great power rivalry in which actors engage each other in degrees of competition, confrontation and conflict (see box

[616] These are types of situations that can occur simultaneously, to varying degrees, in multiple domains, and below the threshold of armed conflict

[617] The government defined composite threats as a term for strategies of competition and confrontation below the threshold of direct armed conflict

[618] Threats can combine diplomatic, informational, military, economic, financial, intelligence and legal means to achieve strategic objectives

[619] The use of agents is often distributed over the long term, and combines overt, covert and hidden methods

[620] Using such means to gain an advantage is not a new phenomenon

[621] In a globalized world with increased competition for power and influence, combined with rapid and groundbreaking technological development, the use of complex instruments has become more common

[622] This challenges national security and poses a security policy risk

[623] Threats can consist of events that appear to be isolated or random, but where the origin turns out to be a security-threatening actor

[624] Activities in the form of espionage, sabotage and influence in the physical, cognitive and cyber domains are tools that state and non-state actors use to exploit potential vulnerabilities

[625] The Armed Forces and the other agencies in the defense sector are highly sought-after targets for complex instruments

[626] National military capabilities and the ability to receive and maintain allies are particularly at risk

[627] Espionage, cyber threats, as well as access and ownership in value chains pose significant challenges for the Armed Forces

[628] The government has initiated a number of measures to address complex threats

[629] The most important single measure is the implementation of the 2019 Security Act with robust preventive security measures

[630] The establishment of the National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) in 2019 has also contributed to increasing digital robustness and resilience

[631] Other examples of concrete measures the government has already implemented are the establishment of the National Intelligence and Security Center (NIS), which is a collaboration between the Police Security Service, the Intelligence Service, the National Security Authority and the police in general

[632] Interdepartmental expert groups have also been established in the areas of influence and screening, and a new law on digital security has been adopted

[633] To meet the ongoing changes in the challenge landscape, the government will further develop measures to identify, assess and respond to complex threats

[634] A concrete measure is a systematic and comprehensive commitment to a robust security service to maintain and protect the Armed Forces in the face of complex threats

[635] The development of a robust security service is discussed in more detail in chapter

[636] The threat from terrorism In NATO's strategic concept from 2022, terrorism has an important place in the threat description

[637] Terrorism is still referred to as the most direct asymmetric threat to peace, security and the citizens of allied countries

[638] The scope for terrorism in Europe has been reduced in recent years as a result of effective counterterrorism work, while at the same time the terrorist threat from militant Islamists has increased

[639] ISIL has attempted to carry out several attacks, and incidents perceived as insults to Islam have contributed to sharpening the threat picture

[640] It is likely that the war between Israel and Hamas will intensify this development

[641] Developments in the Middle East illustrate how quickly the threat can change

[642] The situation highlights the mobilizing power that regional conflicts can have

[643] It also increases the risk that individuals and networks, who would not normally resort to violence against Norwegian and allied interests, may choose to do so

[644] The war between Israel and Hamas has great radicalization potential, and will likely contribute to increasing the terrorist threat in Europe

[645] The development can also be seen in a larger political pattern, where Iran supports Russia's war in Ukraine politically and militarily, and at the same time is a supporter of networks in the Middle East

[646] Instability in other regions could challenge the West's ability to support Ukraine's defense struggle, which would be in Russia's interest

[647] Despite a decline in carried out terrorist attacks by both extreme Islamists and right-wing extremists in Europe in recent years, serious cases of incitement to terrorist attacks, training, and specific attack planning are still being uncovered

[648] Parallel societies in several European countries constitute a recruitment base for the radicalization of youth

[649] In a long-term perspective, the possibility of more solo attacks and attacks from centrally controlled networks must be assumed

[650] Solo attacks are more difficult to uncover than attacks with many people involved

[651] This challenges the authorities' handling

[652] The Islamist terrorist organizations primarily prioritize local growth and attacks in their core areas, and will continue to strengthen themselves in areas with weak government control and local conflicts

[653] The conflict in the Middle East has a mobilizing power whose consequences are difficult to foresee

[654] Norwegian and allied interests have already been affected, and there is a risk that the threat will increase

[655] The Government wants to meet this challenge through closer coordination between Norway, allies and partners

[656] Economic trends

[657] An aging population and the phasing out of petroleum activities will, in the long term, contribute to slowing growth in the Norwegian economy

[658] There are prospects that economic growth will be lower up to 2040 than we have been used to in recent decades

[659] We also see the same trends among important allies, while other countries are expected to experience higher economic growth

[660] This requires clear priorities in the future

[661] Developments in defense spending's share of the state budget and GDP

[662] Share of the state budget (up to 7%) Share of GDP (up to 3%

[663] The share for 2024 is based on the expected allocation level and the Ministry of Finance's GDP forecast as of March

[664] Furthermore, defense spending has been corrected in line with the guidelines for measuring defense spending in NATO

[665] NATO Norway must prepare for reduced room for maneuver in fiscal policy going forward

[666] Public sector costs are expected to increase significantly

[667] The cost increase is mainly due to the increasing proportion of elderly people in the population, leading to increased costs within health and care services and pension payments

[668] The need for labor will increase, while the proportion of residents of working age will decrease

[669] Revenues in the central government budget will grow more slowly as a result of the leveling off of growth in the labor force and the reduction in growth in revenues from the Government Pension Fund Global

[670] Calculations in the 2021 Outlook Report showed that the room for manoeuvre is greatly reduced in the current decade

[671] After 2030, the challenges of increasing expenses due to an aging population will increase

[672] There is reason to believe that there will be less room for use of fund resources in the years ahead than in the past 20 years

[673] The government will present a new Perspective Report during 2024. Maintaining a defense that can handle changing challenges in the current threat landscape requires a continued willingness to invest in the defense sector through stable and predictable financial frameworks

[674] The government wants Norway to spend a minimum of 2 percent of GDP on defense in 2024, and as a minimum maintain this level in the years thereafter

[675] In the decades after the end of the Cold War, the defense sector's share of the state budget and GDP was significantly reduced (see Figure

[676] Successive governments have reversed this trend and increased allocations to the defense sector relative to the state budget

[677] The growth in defense spending has been close to 100 percent since 2010, and defense spending's share of the state budget has increased from 3.6 percent to 4.3 percent during the same period

[678] The deteriorating security situation in Europe, and the world at large, is being met with a significant investment in defense

[679] Social and demographic trends The composition of the population is changing

[680] We are living longer and the proportion of elderly people in society is increasing, while fewer children are being born

[681] In the coming years, this could result in a shortage of expertise and labor within many sectors of society

[682] The defense sector will also face such shortages at a time when security policy changes mean that the Defense Forces will become larger

[683] The economic, social and demographic developments in Norway therefore have significant implications for the country's preparedness and defense capabilities

[684] Increased life expectancy and lower birth rates put pressure on society's shared resources and necessitate clear priorities in the public sector

[685] An aging population combined with a lower proportion of working people is simultaneously increasing competition for smart minds

[686] The gap between the need for, and the availability of, labor is particularly noticeable in rural areas

[687] Many municipalities are experiencing reduced population growth and an increased average age as a consequence of younger people often settling in the cities, while older people remain

[688] Lack of manpower, expertise and capacity is evident in many areas of great importance from a defense and emergency preparedness perspective

[689] For the Armed Forces, the settlement pattern challenges the ability to staff and support operational departments located in the districts

[690] There is a need for flexible and targeted measures to stimulate geographical mobility throughout the sector

[691] A high level of education in the population gives the Norwegian labor market a good starting point for meeting society's future skills needs

[692] Application numbers for higher education indicate that interest in science is declining

[693] The number of study places in technology education programs has remained largely unchanged in recent years

[694] In the long term, these educational trends will create opportunities and limitations for how technology is understood and utilized in society

[695] Labor market surveys indicate that the dynamics between employer and employee increasingly favor workers, especially those with in-demand skills and experience

[696] Younger workers seek individual freedom and expect flexibility

[697] Frequent personnel turnover is more common in many industries than before

[698] Studies also indicate that more factors than salary and skills are important in determining which employers and professions young people apply to

[699] Particular emphasis is placed on the workplace's social and environmental values

[801] NATO's revitalization

[802] The foundation of Norwegian security has been our alliance affiliation with NATO since the Second World War

[803] NATO is both a political and military defense alliance, where member countries are in solidarity and mutually obligated to contribute to defending each other's territory, values, and interests

[804] NATO has an integrated military command structure, joint defense planning, and permanently available decision-making mechanisms

[805] It is therefore of crucial importance to Norway that NATO has the necessary deterrence and defense capabilities to fulfill its core tasks

[806] This applies in particular to collective defense of the member states

[807] NATO has revitalized collective defense

[808] This has also led to increased allied interest in situational awareness and presence in our immediate areas

[809] The comprehensive concept for deterrence and defence of the alliance, decided in 2020, identified Russia and terrorism as the main threats to allied security

[810] This is followed up through NATO's operational planning, NATO's joint command structure and through the link to the member countries' military forces

[811] The changes involve a new approach to the alliance's collective defense

[812] The need for coordination of peacetime activities has increased, and larger parts of the countries' military forces are directly linked to the planning system

[813] This gives increased expectations for the forces' readiness and availability

[814] For Norway, this means increased expectations for capacity, volume, flexibility, preparedness, availability, infrastructure and host country support

[815] It also places other requirements on the staffing of positions in NATO, interoperability and a closer link between national and allied command structures

[816] At the 2022 summit, NATO adopted a new strategic concept

[817] The concept confirms NATO's priorities in strengthening collective defense, and sets the course for the next ten years

[818] The security landscape is considered to be characterized by strategic competition between the great powers, instability and an increased risk of strategic shocks

[819] Russia, as well as instability in southern areas and an associated terrorist threat, are emphasized as concrete, dimensional threats to NATO

[820] For the first time, the challenges resulting from China's rise are discussed

[821] NATO's three core tasks are deterrence and defense, crisis prevention and management, and security cooperation with partners

[822] All tasks are intended to underpin NATO's collective defense capability

[823] International operations constitute a significantly smaller part of NATO's activities after the withdrawal from Afghanistan, but the alliance and allies will still be required to maintain this capability

[824] NATO now places the greatest emphasis on deterrence and defense capabilities

[825] This means that NATO must have a broad set of available forces, with increased readiness and greater endurance

[826] NATO's deterrence strategy is based on nuclear weapons, conventional forces and missile defense, supported by capabilities in outer space and digital space

[827] Nuclear weapons remain the ultimate security guarantee for the alliance

[828] As long as nuclear weapons exist, NATO will also be a nuclear alliance

[829] Improved integration and coherence between different domains is emphasized

[907] Burden-sharing Burden-sharing in NATO is about the fair distribution of roles, risks and responsibilities between member states

[908] It is generally related to the extent to which the various member states spend sufficient financial resources on defense purposes, meet imposed capability goals, and contribute to NATO's permanent tasks and operations

[956] Box 1.3 Multi-domain operations

[957] NATO assumes that deterrence and defense are achieved through robust and combat-ready forces that have the ability to conduct so-called multi-domain operations (MDO

[958] MDO represents a new application of the military power instrument to address threats that span across sectors and phases

[959] MDO is based on the understanding that there are a number of actors who collectively contribute to achieving military objectives and that all military activities take place through the five operational domains (land, sea, air, space and cyberspace

[960] The consequences of these activities will appear as physical, virtual and/or cognitive effects and changes

[961] MDO is a logical development of joint operations into a more domain-oriented approach that seeks to coordinate military and non-military efforts and activities to achieve timely and synchronized effects and changes that support security and defense policy objectives

[962] It is assumed that the Armed Forces follow NATO and our most important allies in their development within MDO to ensure coordinated further development of operational capability, and to avoid creating friction in operations

[963] The approach to MDO will involve a further development of the current concept of command and control, through an increased degree of cooperation, coordination and synchronization across operational domains and functional areas, and supported by a data-centric approach

[964] At the same time as the planning system is being updated and NATO's command structure is being adapted to a new security situation, operations and implementation of permanent tasks are underway led by both NATO and other Allies, both within and outside NATO's core area

[965] This includes a number of peacetime activities in the alliance

[966] The Government will therefore emphasize military capability over time to both cover our national NATO obligations, while also participating with substantial contributions in operations led by NATO or other allies

[967] Norway's contribution to operations can change at short notice

[968] Currently, the Norwegian Armed Forces are participating with capabilities to the Enhanced Forward Presence (eFP) in Lithuania, NATO's Standing Maritime Task Force 1, NATO's Standing Mine Action Force 1 and NATO's Air Patrol Force in Iceland

[969] In addition, we participate with staff officers in several other missions outside NATO's core area, including in the Balkans and the Middle East

[970] Allied and regional cooperation is becoming more important. Cooperation with allied countries, both bilaterally and multilaterally, contributes to the positive development of defense capabilities

[971] It provides, among other things, access to capabilities and materiel, training, exercises, operations and further development of the ability to cooperate

[972] Bilateral cooperation, and cooperation aimed at reinforcement from close allies, is an important part of the allied dimension in the defense of Norway
